episodes.199870: A squall line developed ahead of a cold front leading to wind damage in southeast NC.
episodes.200113: A cold front pushed through the region within an environment displaying high shear and modest instability, producing thunderstorms capable of damaging wind gusts across coastal waters.
episodes.200175: A cold front extending northeast to southwest across central North Carolina slowly pushed eastwards through the afternoon and evening eventually pushing offshore during the overnight hours of the seventh and into the eighth. Along and out ahead of this front, a line of rain and thunderstorm activity was ongoing across western NC and the Triad during the morning of April seventh. This activity then tracked east through the afternoon and evening impacting all coastal waters. Strong wind gusts were the primary hazard within the strongest storms.
episodes.200233: A line of showers and thunderstorms followed a warm front across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians during the morning of April 3rd. A cold front brought more precipitation into the area the night of the 3rd and then stalled over West Virginia through the morning of the 4th. Showers continued in the vicinity of the boundary, which slid to the south the afternoon of the 4th before being lifted north as a warm front again on the 5th. Another cold front arrived the evening of the 5th and once again stalled over West Virginia. Precipitation eventually tapered off as the front sank to the southeast on the 7th.||A total of three to five inches of rain fell in southeast Ohio. Numerous roads were closed due to flooding and water began to approach some homes as creeks and streams rose out of their banks. Water rescues were eventually needed as vehicles became stranded in flood waters. Portions of Symmes Creek, Raccoon Creek, Duck Creek, Shade River, Little Muskingum River, Muskingum River, and the Hocking River all experienced flooding.
episodes.200699: Pre-front thunderstorms moved across an unstable airmass during the afternoon and evening as a strong 500 mb 55-70 kt jet moved across the area providing additional dynamical support and enhanced unidirectional shear.
episodes.200700: Pre-front thunderstorms moved across an unstable airmass during the afternoon and evening as a strong 500 mb 55-70 kt jet moved across the area providing additional dynamical support and enhanced unidirectional shear.
episodes.200826: A frontal boundary passed through South Florida on April 8th bringing scattered showers and thunderstorms across the region. With passing thunderstorms in the morning, winds became gusty across the local Atlantic waters.
episodes.201480: Torrential rainfall in the first week of April resulted in widespread flash flooding and areal flooding in Western Kentucky. On the synoptic scale, the mid to upper levels featured persistent southwesterly flow across the Ohio and Tennessee River Valleys with broad ridging to the east and a trough to the west. Low-level moisture transport was anomalously strong and consistently pointed towards the region. Precipitable water values were above the 99th percentile for this time of year. The surface front was positioned to our west on the afternoon of the 2nd. The front shifted south on the 3rd into Arkansas-Tennessee, then lifted into Western Kentucky and the Missouri Bootheel on the 4th, before returning to Arkansas-Tennessee on the 5th. WPC had a moderate risk Excessive Rainfall Outlook area over at least some of Western Kentucky each day from April 2nd through the 5th, with southern portions of Western Kentucky rising to a high risk on the 3rd and 5th.||Five day rainfall totals of 7-15 across Western Kentucky from April 2nd-6th, with the highest totals occurring from near Mayfield northeastward to Greenville, produced widespread flash flooding issues and long duration areal flooding. Numerous roads, including many state and county roads, become covered by waters due to the cumulative rainfall totals and swelling of creeks and rivers with extensive areal flooding lingering for upwards of a couple weeks (flooding associated more directly with the mainstem rivers, the Ohio, Mississippi, and Green, are covered in focused episodes). The highest rainfall total recorded in Western Kentucky for the first seven days of April was 15.87in at a Kentucky Mesonet site 4mi north of Benton in Marshall County. Other county highs that exceeded 13in include: 15.64in at the Mayfield 2N COOP in Graves County, 15.31in at the Greenville 6.2WSW CoCoRaHS in Muhlenberg County, 14.99in at the Eddyville 2NNE CoCoRaHS in Lyon County, 14.30in at the Cadiz 4SW Kentucky Mesonet in Trigg County, 14.21in at the Hopkinsville 8.5NNE CoCoRaHS in Christian County, 13.78in at the Fulton 3.3NE CoCoRaHS in Hickman County, 13.23in at the Princeton 2SE Kentucky Mesonet in Caldwell County, and 13.03in at the Madisonville 4S Kentucky Mesonet in Hopkins County. The 4-day rainfall record for the entire NWS Paducah CWA was broken by the Marshall County KY Mesonet site which received 15.59 from April 2nd-5th, exceeding the old record of 15.53 from August 13-16, 2016 in Williamsville, MO. Six counties set new 3-day rainfall records from their April 3rd-5th totals (Christian, Hickman, Lyon, Marshall, Muhlenberg, and Trigg).||The historic flood event in Western Kentucky had road closures and damage documented in every county. In the Purchase Area of Western Kentucky, one of the standout impacts was the devastating flooding from the Clarks River. At Almo, the Clarks River crested slightly lower than the February flood earlier in the year but, with a broader area of repeated rounds of heavy rainfall, impacts were greater in Southeastern McCracken County during the April flood with over a dozen homes sustaining major damage from floodwaters in the Krebs and Oaks communities each. Elsewhere in the Purchase Area, rising waters on Mayfield Creek flooded portions of Graves County and along the Ballard/Carlisle County border. Significant flash flooding occurred in the town of Clinton on consecutive nights and, at one point, all but one of the county roads leading out of Hickman County had flood related closures. Landslide damage occurred in the town of Hickman in Fulton County.||Further east, flooding resulted in closure of The Trace in Land Between the Lakes and blocked off portions of the Hillman Ferry Campground. Several homes and businesses in Princeton had flooding impacts, with several sections of road damaged in town. Christian County had some of the worst impacts as major flooding occurred at both forecast point sites on the S Fork Little River near Hopkinsville. Many homes and businesses were impacted by flooding of the N Fork Little River in the northern/western portions of the city with major flooding of many homes on Donna Dr and Dawn Dr and several businesses in Downtown Hopkinsville. Multiple neighborhoods in Oak Grove had over a dozen homes sustaining major flood damage. The Tradewater River exceeded record flood stage at Olney and rose to over 40 at Providence, leading to widespread flooding in western portions of Hopkins and Webster Counties. Dawson Springs had significant flooding impacts to homes and businesses, along with a multi-day closure of I-69. The Green River basin had sprawling river flooding impacts (the more river adjacent areas covered in its own episode) across the six counties in Western Kentucky that the river flows through. McLean County was 40-50% covered at the peak of the flooding. The Pond River had sprawling long-duration flooding due to heavy rain and Green River backwaters, while Elk Creek, Narge Creek, and Otter Creek spread out over Northeastern Hopkins County mid-month. Flooding from Mock Roy Creek and Deer Creek in Northeastern Webster County caused damage to over a dozen homes in Sebree and near Onton, respectively. Significant flooding of Panther Creek in Daviess County resulted in damage to several homes on US-431 while a notable video of a storm line moving through Daviess County made US-431 look like a coastal community experiencing storm surge. In Henderson County, flooding on Canoe Creek caused damage to several structures in the city of Henderson, while sprawling floodwaters extending along ditches that feed into the Green River resulted in damage to many homes in the town of Reed.||Overall, there were several counties in Western Kentucky which experienced dozens of homes with major flood damage adding up to millions of dollars. Hundreds of state road closures occurred during the peak of the flooding, and areal flooding remained for multiple weeks, especially with the Green River basin. Impacts were long-lasting, with hundreds of homes impacted and hundreds of locations with damage to roads, bridges, and culverts. Numerous water rescues occurred, and two people tragically lost their lives (27m in McCracken and 65m in Trigg).
episodes.201527: A cold front swept through the southern Appalachian region on April 6th, producing several hours of moderate to heavy rainfall in the mountains of east Tennessee and western North Carolina. Runoff from this event resulted in the Pigeon River at Newport going into minor flood stage from late in the evening on April 7th and lasting into the early morning hours on April 8th.
episodes.202105: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a stationary front and area of low pressure April 7 and 8. This activity brought gusty winds to the Chesapeake Bay, Rivers, Atlantic Coastal Waters, and Currituck Sound from the afternoon hours April 7 into the early morning hours of April 8.
episodes.202264: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred offshore Key Largo, Florida, in association with a thunderstorm moving eastward along a pre-frontal trough moving through the Florida Keys.
episodes.203945: Heavy rainfall over a multiday period brought flooding to many rivers across Arkansas. Points along the White, Black, Cache, and Ouachita Rivers remained in flood through the remainder of the month.

events.narrative: Torrential rainfall the first week of April, and backwater from major flooding on the Green River, resulted in flooding of several roads in Northwestern Daviess County. Multiple structures sustained water damage in Newman, while major damage occurred to two homes on KY-279 near Lee Rudy Rd. Most of US-60 west of Owensboro in Daviess County was closed for a time along with portions of KY-1554 south of Stanley and KY-279 south of Griffith.

events.narrative: Several rounds of torrential rainfall the first week of April resulted in widespread flooding issues including along the Pond River that marks the county line between Southwestern McLean County and Hopkins County. KY-85 was covered by floodwaters for an extended period due to major flooding on the Green River slowing the progression of water down the Pond River.

events.county: Webster
events.narrative: Several rounds of heavy rainfall the first week of April, along with backwater onto creeks due to major flooding on the Green River, resulted in flooding issues in Slaughters and Onton. KY-138 heading north and east of Slaughters was closed due to flooding. A bridge over the East Fork Deer Creek was damaged on Slaughters Elmwood Rd. Several homes on KY-370 near and southeast of Onton had water damage, especially near Pitman Creek. Additional homes with flood damage were located on Cox Mill Rd and Sassafras Grove Rd.
